subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXPANSION OF GRANT PROGRAM-MOTION UNDER SO. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, over the past two to three years we have been promised that new and large boundaries and guidelines will be created with respect to regional development incentive grants. In that time nothing has changed despite the fact the expansion of the grant program would provide incentives to industry either to locate in new areas or enlarge existing facilities, thus helping solve the problems of job creation and regional disparity in many areas not now included in the program. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis):
That the minister responsible immediately announce changes involving regional development incentive grants which would result in the establishment of new and enlarged boundaries.

subsubtopic: IMPENDING DECISION OF SKAGIT VALLEY FLOODING-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I, too, rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. On October 9 of last year the International Joint Commission said it would rule today on the fate of the Skagit Valley in British Columbia. The IJC is meeting at this moment behind closed doors in Washington, D.C., and may make a decision without a Canadian chairman because the Liberal government has left the position vacant for over a year. In order to protect the Skagit Valley from being flooded by Liberal indifference, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose):
That this House support the call for public hearings into the Skagit Valley issue, which is supported by all parties in this House, and that because of the Liberal government's failure to appoint a Canadian chairman to the IJC, an allparty committee be struck today to seek a Canadian of high repute who can serve on this important bilateral body.

Madam Speaker, at present gasoline prices in White Rock, British Columbia, are about 30 cents a gallon higher than in the State of Washington just a few miles away. The United States price reflects the world price, whereas gasoline prices in Canada have almost doubled in the last two years, most of the increases reflecting increases in taxation. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp):
That the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources indicate clearly whether it is the policy of the government to make consumers in Canada pay higher than world prices for gasoline to support excessive government taxation which finances programs which do not lead to energy self-sufficiency.

Agreed.

Madam Speaker, in only 28 days Canadians will have to file their 1981 income tax returns under threat of heavy fine and imprisonment should they fail to comply. However, the government has not even introduced the tax legislation emanating from the ill-conceived November budget which will dictate the taxes people will be forced to pay. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn):

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF RESEARCH COUNCIL-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Canada, indeed the whole industrialized world, is sitting on an environmental time bomb. The very health and welfare of our children and of our children's children are at stake depending on, whether we act now to halt the poisoning of the planet, and how this is done. Dioxin, acid rain, PCBs, methyl mercury, and captan are only the tip of the iceberg, not to mention the stuff we deliberately put in our food, such as red dye No. 2 and sodium nitrite. Therefore 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton):
That this House instruct the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the cabinet in general to consider the setting up of an independent national hazardous substances research council so that we can begin to make such research a priority to prepare ourselves for an already risky future, and that this research be partially funded by a levy on all the corporations which, over the years, have so carelessly and selfishly endangered the future of human life in the idolatrous pursuit of profit.

Madam Speaker, Canada's 1982 Great Lakes shipping season starts Monday under a very serious cloud of uncertainty. The number of ships coming through the Great Lakes is down by estimates ranging up to 25 per cent of the total fleet. Lower levels of economic activity and higher energy costs are cited as being among the major reasons for the slump. Given the impact of high energy costs on water-borne commerce, particularly accentuated by the discriminatory marine fuels surcharge tax, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby):
That the government take immediate steps to roll back or rescind the discriminatory tax on Canada's shipping fleet so that it might be restored to its full competitive position.

subsubtopic: ARGENTINA-REPORTED INVASION OF FALKLAND ISLANDS- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. I note that this morning's news includes reports that Argentinian troops have landed and claimed possession of the Falkland Islands, historically a British protectorate. Ninety-eight per cent of the residents are of British descent and they have expressed a desire to maintain their British roots. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers):
That this House resoundingly condemn Argentina for its overt military aggression and send a letter of protest to the President of Argentina requesting the immediate withdrawal of military forces so that a peaceful and democratic solution to this conflict may be attained.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question to the Prime Minister is supplementary to the questions previously asked. The other day the Prime Minister suggested that Canadians should follow the 163 Ways and Means motions presently filed as a result of the November 12 budget, in preparing their income tax returns. The Prime Minister failed to mention that there were no ways and means motions filed with respect to the December 18 statement. There have been other statements by the Minister of Finance across the country. There is speculation everywhere that changes are going to be made or have been made.
Could the Prime Minister tell this House if and when new ways and means motions are going to be filed, so that people can have some understanding of where they are going? The Prime Minister must realize the uncertainty that is being caused by the general feeling that this budget is causing great damage to the community.

speechtext: The Department of National Revenue is in chaos.

Madam Speaker, will the Prime Minister tell a tourist operator, for example, filing his 1981 tax return, what kind of capital cost allowance he is allowed in filing that return? When he buys a lamp, towel or something of that nature, does he write it off in full as the old law says, or is it half capital cost allowance? What do those who were students do with respect to money they thought they were getting back on their returns which they planned to use to pay their student loans? speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am not surprised if there is confusion in the minds of the people of Canada, because the opposition has been endeavouring for the past three months to create that confusion. I wish they would follow the time-honoured rules of taking the budget statements and the dates announced there for tax changes as the rules. There have been changes to every budget since I have been here. There are always some amendments, whether it be in one or another aspect of the bills, that are accepted. speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Yesterday the Ontario environment ministry found in a study that dioxin levels in Lake Ontario are the highest they have ever been. The study showed there were 27.4 parts per trillion of dioxin found in trout, and 59 parts per trillion found in minnows, in the Port Credit area. Will the minister advise Canadians who live in that community and who fish in Lake Ontario, in the immediate area of Port Credit, if in her opinion it is advisable for them to continue to eat fish found in Lake Ontario?

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT MARINE FUEL SURTAX BE RESCINDED
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. The government will be fully aware of the very serious decline in the number of Great Lake ships which will leave for the Seaway when it opens on Monday. To a large measure this is due to the marine fuel surcharge. At jeopardy here is not only the lowered activity of the Great Lakes fleet but it is, in a very direct way, a threat to the jobs of 1,100 and upwards to 1,700 Canadian seamen. Would the government consider, as a serious step to protect those jobs and enhance the competitive position of the Canadian Great Lakes fleet, rescinding or rolling back the very significant marine fuel surcharge tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT MARINE FUEL SURTAX BE RESCINDED

Madam Speaker, I would like to remind the hon. member, first, that there is no surcharge on Canadian lake ships employed in shipping between Canadian ports. The surcharge applies only when oil is used for international trips, and it applies equally to American or Canadian ships on the same basis. At the present time this charge is rather minimal, as a matter of fact.
I remind my hon. friend that all over North America the transportation industry generally is facing a difficult situation. This applies to railways, trucking, airways, and the shipping industry in general. The industry is having a difficult time, but not because of the cost of fuel. It is because of a slowdown in the economy generally in North America as well as in Europe. subsubtopic: LEVYING OF TAX ON WORLD PRICES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, and is supplementary to the question by the member for Dartmouth-Halifax East.
Could the minister inform the House whether he agrees with statements made by representatives of the Canadian shipping industry who held a convention here in Ottawa this week? They felt that levying the surcharge on marine fuel expended on international voyages in inland waters on Canadian entrepreneurs was discriminatory, and also that the surcharge was an infringement of the National Transportation Act, since it applied only to marine transportation and not to railway or highway transportation, and finally, that a large part of the traffic in American goods carried by Canadian entrepreneurs would now be carried by American shippers who, as a result of the surcharge would now be economically more attractive.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mare Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: LEVYING OF TAX ON WORLD PRICES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I must say I disagree with this assumption. First of all, we must not forget that there are certain taxes for land carriers, for instance trucks, which are different from those levied on marine carriers. We have always had taxation systems that varied depending on the type of transportation.
As far as international transportation is concerned, we have the same arrangement for American and Canadian ships, but there is no evidence that this factor has had any effect on the preference for Canadian or American carriers in international transportation.
Finally, I should like to remind my colleague that Canadian carriers have a considerable advantage in Canadian ports, and that this advantage could be put to good competitive use, even on international routes.

Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. It concerns a tax rip-off of about 18 cents a gallon to Canada's oil consumers. Why, in his announcement yesterday, did the minister not change the flat rate compensation formula, which does not consider the actual cost of imported crude but only the average, thereby today over-compensating certain oil refiners and oil importers in eastern Canada by as much as $9 a barrel?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am afraid my hon. friend does
Oral Questions
not understand the oil compensation charge very well. As he says, it is an average, and for every cent of advantage that a particular refiner might get on a cargo, he or his competitors will lose an equivalent cent on other cargoes because the charge is an average. The total net result, as far as importers are concerned, is exactly zero. For any money they will make on one cargo they, or somebody else, will lose it on another cargo, so there is no advantage over-all in terms of the import compensation charge.

Madam Speaker, perhaps I do not understand the complexities of the oil compensation charge, but I certainly do not understand the minister either, because the minister has come out with a policy to reduce exports, reduce prices, involve himself in swaps, and all the rest of it. If it does not make any difference, why bother?

Madam Speaker, will the minister assure the House that he will institute either a better reporting system, involve himself in complete swaps, or at least, if there is over-compensation, institute a rebate so that the consumer can get money back from the over-subsidizing of oil importers in eastern Canada?

1.	What is the current government policy on strikes in the public service and Crown corporations, particularly in essential services?
2.	Has the government considered or is it considering changes in the present legislation, limiting the right to strike in essential services and substituting some other method of settling labour problems?

speakeroldname: Mr. David Smith (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am informed by Treasury Board of Canada and Labour Canada as follows:
1.	The Public Service Staff Relations Act, which received all party support when first passed in 1967, allows bargaining agents representing employees of the federal government to choose conciliation/strike as the dispute resolution method. The government respects that right. Section 79(1) of the Public Service Staff Relations Act also provides:
"Notwithstanding Section 78 (concerning the establishment of a conciliation board), no conciliation board shall be established for the investigation and conciliation of a dispute in respect of a bargaining unit until the parties have agreed on, or the board has determined pursuant to this section the employees or classes of employees in the bargaining unit (hereinafter in this act referred to as "designated employees") whose duties consist in whole or in part of duties the performance of which at any particular time or after any specified period of time is or will be necessary in the interest of the safety or security of the public."
Section 101(1) of the same act provides:
"No employee shall participate in a strike-
(c) who is a designated employee"
It is to be noted that the act refers to "duties . . . necessary in the interest of the safety or security of the public and not 'essential services'."
The current government policy on strikes in the public service is to endeavour, in negotiating with its employees, to avoid strikes. However, where agreement cannot be reached through direct negotiation and where the bargaining agent has chosen the conciliation/strike route, then the provisions of Sections 79 and 101 of the Public Service Staff Relations Act with respect to safety or security of the public apply.
Crown corporations are under the Canada Labour Code and thus the provisions of the PSSRA do not apply.
2.	The government is presently reviewing legislation concerning collective bargaining in the federal public service. That legislative review includes a review of the framework of

April 2, 1982
Order Paper Questions
collective bargaining and the processes for the resolution of disputes. As a result of the review, the government will be proposing, in due course, appropriate amendments to the Public Service Staff Relations Act and other legislation which may be affected.
Labour Canada
1- With respect to strikes involving Crown corporations, the government fully supports the free collective bargaining process, including the right of employees to withdraw their services or the employer to lock out his employees. Part V of the Canada Labour Code contains provisions which place certain requirements on the bargaining parties before lawful strike or lock-out action may be initiated; these include the filing of a notice of dispute with the Minister of Labour and the exhaustion of all conciliation assistance available to the parties at the discretion of the Minister of Labour. In addition, the code effectively prohibits strikes over rights disputes and on the question of union recognition, and allows for limiting the acquisition of the right to strike or lock out when Parliament is dissolved.
In instances where contract negotiations reach an impasse, the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service of Labour Canada provides expert conciliation and mediation assistance to the parties in an attempt to resolve their differences and arrive at a mutually satisfactory agreement. The vast majority of disputes referred to FMCS are settled without resort to strike or lock-out action.
2. The government is not considering changes in the present legislation with regard to
(a)	the acquisition and exercise of the right to strike; and
(b)	the mediation and conciliation procedures for the resolution of disputes
with respect to the collective bargaining process in Crown corporations.

He said: Madam Speaker, as you will see from the text of the motion, its purpose is to focus attention upon major government policies, particularly those of an economic nature, or which impact directly on our economy.
I might say by way of introduction that government policies are the result of the exercise of political power. I would be hard pressed to find a government, indeed a political party, more obsessed with political power than the one opposite me. Unhappily, I believe it has been this obsession which has obscured and distorted the use of power. Without oversimplifying the matter, I suggest to you that political power is nothing more or less than the right and responsibility of a government to provide services to people. As a result of the exercise of political power, and implementation of government policy flowing from it, services should be delivered to Canadians.
They may be, Mr. Speaker, Canadians in a particular region where a government policy enhances the opportunities of the people in that region. They may be Canadians in a particular strata of society who are being assisted; the poor or disabled, for example. They may be Canadians in a certain sector of our society, such as farmers or manufacturers, or they may be social policies which would be of benefit to all Canadians.
The point is that, with very few exceptions, government policies should operate to benefit Canadians. I am not only sepaking of the expenditure by the government of the tax dollars that it has collected, because the government may opt to create, for example, a climate of opportunity, or a climate of challenge, or a climate of optimism, which is often much more effective and beneficial than the expenditure of billions of taxpayers' dollars.
What has prompted this particular motion is that recently major government policies have done exactly the opposite to what they were supposed to do and what they have traditionally and historically done. Instead of creating benefits and
April 2, 1982

beneficiaries, the government has created casualties and victims by the thousands, by the tens of thousands and by the hundreds of thousands. One casualty list alone has over one million names on it. That is the list of jobless casualties. They are in every region, in every sector and in every strata. They may be fishermen in our coastal waters or farmers in our rural areas. They may be miners, they may be factory workers, they may be the young who are trying to enter the job market or they may be the elderly on fixed incomes. It is in this area that we differ with our colleagues to the right. I am not sure whether they advocate lowering interest rates, maintaining interest rates as they are or increasing them, because I hear hon. members talking about all three options.
They support the banks.
I do not know what on earth they are recommending. It depends which speaker is making a speech and to whom he is making it.
What would you do about interest rates, Nelson?

Interest rates have to be lowered as part of an over-all industrial strategy. If they are not lowered, we cannot expect a rejuvenation of our economy or a recovery to occur. Without a reduction of interest rates, economic recovery is impossible. I ask hon. members to ask themselves a question. Why is it that interest rates in Japan can be 7 per cent or 8 per cent?
You tell us.

Why does any Japanese investor invest anything in Japan when he could bring his money to Canada and obtain a 20 per cent return? How can interest rates in Japan be 7 per cent? The reason is that the Japanese have a comprehensive industrial strategy in place. The Japanese have a government which is able to develop co-operation between labour, management, financial institutions and the government. That is something we do not have in this country, and at this moment we certainly have a long way to go toward developing that cooperation.
A comprehensive industrial strategy, including the reduction of interest rates, is the way to begin to turn the present recessionary trend around and the way to begin to develop confidence in our future.

That was all very specific.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, unaccustomed as I am to this wild applause-
Hear, hear!

But in a more serious vein, today we are being treated to the likes of an opposition resolution which is designed to condemn the government for all sins of omission and commission and what other miscellaneous things they can find. I want to say though that the traditional routine to which we are usually subjected on Fridays has been somewhat enlivened by the highly theatrical performance of the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Jarvis). It befits the member who represents that centre of Canadian theatre, Stratford. It is appropriate the opposition sees fit to appoint someone who is so talented in the ways of the theatrical arts. It is the only way in which they can make their case convincing because there is actually no substance to what they have to say. They have to hide everything by using all kinds of wiles and guiles, of which only the member from Perth is capable.
When the hon. member talks about the problems of unemployment and when one considers his performance, I think a second career is called for on the stage at Stratford, not here. However, this brings to mind a quote from Macbeth, of which I am sure the hon. member for Perth will be aware. It reads:
Away and mock the time with fairest show. False face must hide what the false heart doth know.
I would say that is exactly what we have before us. Judging by the subterfuge that is being presented by members opposite, it appears they are trying to present a case they know is not there. It is unfortunate that we are being treated to this theatrical performance as opposed to a serious debate. We all know how serious the situation is. We all know this country, along with many others, is facing a recessionary period. There is a serious downturn in employment. There is still an unacceptable rate of inflation. There are still a number of turbulences in the economy which must be straightened out and dealt with. 1 do not think it is to anyone's benefit to keep hearing what the hon. member for Perth and the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) keep saying, namely that it is the government's fault. It is a question for which we as a government take some responsibility. Certainly there are many

April 2, 1982
Supply
others in this country who must share more of the responsibility for what has happened. But they must also share the responsibility for solutions.
We on this side of the House say constantly that we are ready, willing, and prepared to co-operate and join in partnership with the business community, with trade unions, with the opposition and with financiers in order that together we can come to grips with things during these difficult times. That cannot happen, Mr. Speaker, if the whole point and objective of the opposition is to create division and fractiousness; to create false alarms which constantly frighten people into stampedes in the hope that they will gain some momentary or temporary political advantage, as opposed to offering some reasonable and rational solutions to the problems.
This is unfortunate because the times call for more serious leadership than this. We are always being presented with blanket condemnations. When members get to the end of their speeches they say they will talk about the solutions. Before that happens, though, we have 28 and a half minutes of vitriol and fulminations about the perfidy of the Liberal government, and in the last minute or so we hear "I think we have a solution, but I am sorry, I cannot give it to you because I have run out of time". That is a classic example of what we hear in this House day in and day out. We hear "Boy, do we have problems, and if you would only give us the chance, we would give you the answers, except that we have just run out of time".
I have been through several opposition days in the last two or three months as befits my own position as Minister of Employment and Immigration. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I am waiting to hear members of the opposition say something that makes sense. When members of the opposition can solve their own internal contradictions and resolve their own basic inherent conflicts in their caucuses, perhaps then we will have a clear and consistent position from the opposition as to what they think should be done.
On the one hand, we have the financial critic for the Conservative party who gave a speech in Toronto who said the only answer for Canada is Reaganomics. He said: In other words, "Let us do what President Reagan is doing and slash, cut and tie everything down. Let us go back to the Reagan formula, cut back social services, social welfare, training, employment-cut back everything". That is his answer.
Absolutely the opposite.

Now we hear the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Jarvis) saying "Absolutely the opposite"-let us spend more money, let us do more. Let us stimulate. Let us have incentives. Let us have cash incentives. Let us do all of these other things. Well, who are we to believe? Who speaks for the Conservative party here?
Let me give another example. We have the hon. member for Perth decrying with the most eloquent crocodile tears the failures of the megaprojects. He says, "My riding is suffering because the Liberal government could not get an agreement with the Alberta government." He does not mention Shell,
Gulf, or any other companies who are the ones who are actually pulling out of these projects, even though we are offering substantial subsidies and incentives. The hon. member says that it is their responsibility, and he asks: "What can we do about it? Let us get something going that will create work in my riding and in other ridings."
It was only a week ago today that I was in this very House debating an opposition resolution on transportation. I listened to the outrage and the outcrying of members of the Conservative and New Democratic parties, who kept saying, "Do not modernize the transportation system. Do not go ahead and spend $17 billion, even though by doing that it would create work in southwestern Ontario and right across the country." Modernizing the railway system would create $17 billion of investment and provide tens of thousands of jobs for Canadians.
That was the position they took last Friday. This Friday the hon. member for Perth says: "Go ahead and do it. Let us get the megaprojects on the road." Last Friday they told us not to go ahead and do that. I do not know what has happened in the last week. Maybe they had a caucus meeting and decided that today was turnaround time. But it simply comes down to the unalterable fact that we cannot find out what the Conservative Party wants to do.
Neither can they.

That is the problem, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne) just took away my punch line. The reason we do not know what the Conservatives want is that they do not know what they want either. It is endemic of that party. What they are doing is trying to tiptoe through these difficult times hoping that no one will find out that they have an internal mass of contradictions that are wrapped up in an enigma, led by a person who is less than an enigma.
We are trying to debate the serious topic of economic growth and development. We are looking for an opposition day to at least provide us with the kinds of answers that we think would enhance our sense of direction. They say they know what to do, yet all we see is this constant inability to have at least a consistent line of argument. So, Mr. Speaker, if at times we have a certain degree of skepticism about their sincerity and willingness to come to grips with the problem, I think it is justified. Every time we look at what they have to say, all we see are contradictions or gross exaggerations. The hon. member for Perth is guilty of the parliamentary sin of trying to create a sense of hysteria by using false figures. He says there is going to be a billion dollar deficit in the UIC fund which we will have to bail out. Where did he get those figures from? In fact, last year we had a $350 million surplus in the fund. We then reduced the premiums by 15 cents per $100 of salary. It is our estimate that even if unemployment averaged 9 per cent for the entire year-which it will not-the total additional cost would be $400 million to $500 million, which

means any extra premium cost would only be what we reduced the premiums by this year.
Now, that is an estimate, a judgment. We do not begin to forecast what the fund will be until the third quarter, but the hon. member for Perth has his own little abacus back there where he adds things up and gets this magical $1 billion deficit figure. Well, that is irresponsible, and I charge the hon. member with being irresponsible for using those kinds of figures. He has no business doing it, and he knows better because he is generally a responsible member of this House. However, 1 think he is getting carried away in a sort of caucus euphoria where they say we have tough times, let us see if we can burrow and dig and make things a little worse by using this kind of false figure. That is not the way to deal with serious conditions in a serious time. What we should be dealing with is realistic members, looking at the real problems and trying to come up with real answers.
At the same time we are also dealing with a situation where the Conservative party keeps fuelling the fire of its sins by insisting that somehow it has an answer for high interest rates even though as a government it was in favour of them. The Conservatives recognized-and I give them credit for it-that this is not a problem isolated to Canada; it is one which every industrialized country of the world is facing. So looking at this resolution which says the government is responsible for lay-offs and so on, if they use some sense of logic-and 1 hate to try and convince the opposition to use logic because I know it is a practice foreign to them-they would have to follow through and say that the American, British and German governments, indeed all governments, are dead wrong in their policies. Whether they be Social Democrats, Republicans, Conservatives, Socialists or Liberals, they are all wrong. Which means the only people who are right must be the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada.
You have got it.

They are the only ones who have the answer-except we have not yet heard it, Mr. Speaker. So they are going to keep us wondering for another opposition day, and another one beyond that.
The fact of the matter is, Mr. Speaker, that if we want to come to grips with these issues, as do members on this side, let us at least be honest about it and deal with facts and reality, not the fiction and fantasy which appears every time we look at one of their resolutions. Let us deal with what is happening in Canada and with what kinds of solutions might be available.
The NDP finance critic says we do not have any policy, there is nothing there. Well, let us examine that because I think there are some interesting contradictions among our friends in the NDP as well. I wonder what their strategy is. One day I hear from the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) that we are not doing enough to bring people into the country;

let us bring in more refugees and help these different groups of people overseas.
Jim Coutts will take care of him.
We are certainly hopeful of that.
You will be hoping for a long time.

The concern over immigrants is legitimate and one we respond to. But then last week the hon. member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Keeper) said that this government is engaged in dastardly deeds; it is bringing in skilled workers. You cannot have it both ways, Mr. Speaker. They cannot say one day, "bring more people in", and the next day, "stop bringing in anyone at all". We have a situation, Mr. Speaker, where the NDP finance critic said: "Our strategy is to go for the growth industries; let us go for the winners in society, the guys who are on the way up." All right, I will buy that, but is it not exceedingly strange that the NDP, the great spokesmen for the working man, are prepared to forget the hundreds of thousands of workers in other industries who must also be protected? Is it not odd that this party, which carries the banner of labour and in fact does their bidding, is prepared to forget about the textile, footwear and garment industries, which are in some decline? They are not prepared to offer any assistance to them whatsoever.
Well, we are not as heartless as they are because we have an industrial strategy which is aiming to provide grants to help those industries develop new equipment and technology. At the same time we have introduced a number of programs to help workers affected by changeovers to adjust. There is a $350 million program for industrial labour adjustment which is now in operation in many communities represented by NDP members to help workers be retrained for new jobs.
The New Democratic Party members forget about things like that, Mr. Speaker. They do not want to talk about the worker whose only real security is in his or her skill. Oh, no, this is a party totally indifferent to skill training in Canada. 1 do not hear them congratulating this government when we increase the budget for skill training by 18 per cent this year alone, so that we will be spending over $1 billion this year and adding thousands of opportunities for workers to be retrained. What do we get from the NDP for that? They say, "Oh, that is not good enough; it is a gimmick, a trick, do not listen to them." What do we get from the president of the CLC? the government is spending $1 billion to help retrain workers in Canada. We do not care about retraining or adjustment."

-to provide for the development of a new technology industry. But at the same time this same government is also employing a program to help the textile and footwear industries. We are providing major assistance in places like Cambridge and Brant.

I ask the NDP to go back to those areas and speak to those workers who are signing an average of 20 or 30 agreements a week, and ask them if they think it is a gimmick that we are saving their jobs and keeping them employed. Is that so much of a gimmick? Is that part of the NDP's callousness toward the workers, showing that it does not care that we are saving jobs?
What we are pointing out is that this kind of emotion which is constantly erupting on opposition days is not really based upon the reality of what we are trying to do in this country. This is evident, because we do admit we have difficult times and we have hard times; but we are also saying that we are trying to work our way out of it. At the same time we are trying to provide protection and security for working people.
You got us into it.

Let me consider another statement by the finance critic for the NDP which I think will be of enormous amusement to everyone in this House. He said, "I will give you the motto if you wish it followed. Let us do what the Japanese do." The Japanese have been pretty successful. Has the hon. member really considered the way the Japanese society is organized? Does he know that it is a fully corporate society where the large corporations make the decisions behind closed doors with government? This is the party whose leader stands up, day after day, and yells and screams and goes into a tantrum about the multicorporate state and the dominance of the American corporations; but now his finance critic is saying, "Why do we not do what the Japanese do and get that secretive corporate state together?"
American is bad. Japanese is good.

That is right. Somehow, the Japanese corporate society is okay, but if an American corporation tries to do something here, it is no good.
Again, we come back to the point that we would like to be able to listen with some respect to the propositions put forward by the members of the opposition. But surely, when we are faced with those kinds of statements, when one day they say zig and the next day they say zag, when one day they are up and the next day they are down, when one day they are left and the next day they are right, we do not know who speaks for whom. It is truly the party of total individualism because each of its members says something different.
We must find a more realistic approach. As we have said in this House many times, we have provided a budget and an economic program that we believe will make a difference in this country.
Yes, it sure will.
It will make a big difference. It has already made a difference. It killed us!
That is right. It is making a difference because the inflation rate has come down in the last two months.
It is 11.6 per cent.

The inflationary pressures are being reduced. We realize there is still a problem on the horizon. We still realize that a number of highly inflated wage settlements are being considered, and some of the major sons in the CLC are saying, "No truck or trade with anyone, boy, we are going for broke!" There is no co-operation, no partnership and no attempt to compromise. They are saying, "We are going straight down the line for what we want. We do not care about anyone else. We do not care about the country. We do not care about industry. It can go broke, for all we care. We are just going for the big bundle." That is what we are beginning to hear from the political masters of the NDP and from the CLC

executive. We must face that problem and find some resolution.
The hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap said something which I thought was kind of intriguing. Maybe he gave us some kind of a clue as to what the NDP is really after. He said that what we have to do is go to a wartime footing. Whenever there is wartime there are wage and price controls. Emergency powers.

Oh, oh!

Sure you would.

I agree we are in difficult times, but this government is not prepared to go to wage and price controls at this time. We would prefer to have voluntary restraint. We would prefer that business, labour and government each showed a sign of restraint.
Get them together.

We have taken our first step by putting forward a budget which shows that restraint. Through that restraint we will bring inflation rates down and, by bringing inflation rates down, we will bring high interest rates down.
Are they bringing them down?

There is no artificial mucking around. Rather, we are doing it on the basis that that is the system from which there will be a natural market decision to bring the rates down, not an artificial decision which would produce all kinds of convulsions in international trade and in the flow of finances out of this country, and which would cause a higher rate of inflation because we would have to import products at higher cost from abroad.
That is what has happened.

That is the kind of position we are taking. It has put forward the basic element that we must stimulate research and development. I fully agree with the finance critic of the NDP. R and D is indeed important. That is one reason we have increased the budget of the National Science Engineering Council by 21 per cent this year. We have increased the budget of the Medical Research Council by

23 per cent. We put $436 million into the aerospace program and an additional $100 million toward the Telidon program. Therefore, there is agreement that that is a major area of investment.
It is the reason that our envelope of economic development commits $60 billion of government investment to provide incentives and subsidies in support of private industry in this country. We need a change in the tax system.

But at the same time, we believe that we must go beyond that. We must have a basic framework of restraint. We must see that those investments are strategically placed in those areas where they will have the maximum impact. However, we also need major co-operation from the other economic actors; we cannot do it alone. The government does not run the entire economy, it is run by all departments. Thousands of decisions are being made every day by businessmen, by trade unions and by provincial governments, which spend far more of the national purse than we do. If one adds up the provincial budgets, they have a much higher public expenditure than the federal government.
That is why you need cooperative federalism. You should never say it is dead.

That is right. That is why we we need better federalism and have tried to come to better arrangements in those areas. Therefore, we see there is a need for economic strategy.
I refer hon. members to the paper which was tabled at the time of the budget. It sets out the basic element of that strategy. That is what we should be debating today. manner we have heard in the debate thus far. Our basic thrust in these difficult times is to develop some kind of confidence and to use the tax system.

The current outlook, Mr. Speaker, no matter how you look at it, whether from government sources or private sources, is very bleak; it is negative and frightening for the average Canadian. Statistics Canada in February warned that a current recovery is not imminent, that all indicators are negative and continuing to decline. In March they said a recovery is not yet imminent. Nothing really has changed. The outlook for exports, according to Statistics Canada, is not good for the automotive sector, particularly as it pertains to Ontario, and also the manufacturing sector is extremely bleak.
I suggest that in April we will have roughly the same kind of scenario, that a turnaround in the economy is still not imminent.
The outlook is bleak, and that comes not only from government sources but other sources. One of the reasons is that we are still continuing to have double-digit inflation, and interest rates that are astronomical by any standards. I will mention more about interest rates and their effect later on in my remarks.
Unemployment in this country is far too high. The decline in business investment and the weakness in the United States on which our economy depends to a large extent rules out the possibility of a quick turnaround in economic activity. For many Canadians this means disaster, not only disaster with regard to their job in the coming year, but their homes and, most important, the dignity with which they conduct their affairs.
We know what brought this on. It is a combination of many things. We are paying for past sins. Government spending is far too high and it is still climbing. Inflation, which is part of the whole question of government spending, is running far in excess of what it should be.
There is a lack of confidence in the government. In some cases people do not trust any political parties. They certainly do not trust the government in giving economic leadership. I am not necessarily saying Canadians should follow that leadership, but the leadership should be there. It is not at the present time.
The economic situation is so bad that every day the government has to borrow $30 million. It is spending money it does not have. In order to borrow that kind of money, it has to compete. It competes with the private sector and with individual Canadians who must borrow money for mortgages and capital projects. The government, which is the regulator in our society, is one of the main purchasers of money in the marketplace. Canadians must compete with the government. If Canadians followed the same kind of spending program as the government, they would be broke.
This year Canadian taxpayers must pay $17 billion to service the national debt. This figure comes from the spending estimates tabled in this House by the government. The debt service charge is increased by $2.1 billion over last year. It represents 22 per cent of the total outlay of $76.3 billion. It is significant that the size of the expenditure is about ten times

April 2, 1982
Supply
the amount the government will spend on economic development.
In spite of this expenditure to service our debt, we are not getting ahead; it just pays the interest. It is similar to the situation of someone who has borrowed to the maximum from his bank and can get no further credit, so he goes to another bank to make a loan to pay the first bank. This government has gone to a whole series of banks around the world. We are not only mortgaging what is being done at present, but mortgaging the future of our young Canadians.
The public debt charge is the fastest growing area in government expenditures. The government must borrow more money simply to pay the interest on the $122 billion it now owes. If a business borrowed in that manner, it would soon go bankrupt.
Other members who have spoken in this debate today have dealt with the matter of where the money should be spent. In times such as this, there are basically two areas. Money should be spent to help those who cannot for various reasons help themselves. People require help because they have been hurt by inflation, a stagnating economy and the stumbling and bumbling by the government through its budget and other tax proposals. It is absolutely necessary to target money for housing and other such areas.
On the other side of the coin, the government through the tax system and tax incentives should give encouragement and direction to the productive sectors of the economy. One that I am keenly aware of and know something about is the agricultural sector. Over the last number of years we have lost the ability to compete in world markets for a good many products. Canada has the potential to become a superpower in one area, much like Japan and West Germany have become superpowers in some instances. That area is agriculture. We can produce food more efficiently than most countries in the world. We can produce it on a par with the United States.
If we are going to excel, we must have an industrial strategy. We must attack the areas of greatest potential in our economy, as the Japanese and West Germans have. If we are going to capitalize, it should be in this area. We have lost to other countries in electronics, notably radio and television, and in automobiles. We are having problems trying to keep down auto imports as consumers want to buy other than what is produced in this country.
We could become a superpower in agriculture. We should direct our attention to that area and develop an industrial strategy aimed at agriculture. About 4 per cent of the population produces the food, but approximately 40 per cent of the total economic activity in this country is a derivative of agriculture or an agriculture-related activity. This is not happening at the present time. We are not directing our efforts toward an industry in which we could be the best. It is unfortunate, but I believe that the United States will take away more of our markets.
We have the potential to be a superpower in agriculture. However, the government is not giving it the proper attention which it should. Nation wide farm bankruptcies are up this year from last year by 75 per cent in January and 54 per cent in February. Although the figures are not out yet, the number of bankruptcies will be high in March and probably just as high in April and May.
Many farmers discover that they cannot finance their operations to put seed, fertilizer and chemicals into the ground for the spring. This is a shocking situation and unfortunately it is only the tip of the iceberg. However, it is the best indicator of the situation which is developing within the agricultural sector. Many farmers are being forced out of business either by foreclosures or by sales. Farm costs in western Canada have increased by almost 12 per cent. Over the past decade farm costs have run at over 300 per cent. This is largely due, certainly within the last few years, to a 635 per cent increase in interest charges on farm debt.
I know of very few other sectors of our economy which uses capital in the way the agricultural sector does. Agricultural authorities estimate that in 1982 the cost of farm input will increase by at least 10 per cent while net incomes will decline by an enormous 15 per cent. The gap is beginning to widen to such an extent that many agricultural producers are no longer caught in a squeeze, they are in a death grip. We must keep in mind that if one industry in this country is capable of turning our GNP around and generate economic activity, it is the agricultural industry because Canadian farmers can produce agricultural products better than any other country in the world.
All other costs related to farm production have also risen significantly. For example, the cost of machinery is up by almost 20 per cent, building and fencing costs are up approximately 12 per cent, supply and services rose 20 per cent and crop production input costs rose 14 per cent. All this occurs during a period of declining real income for farmers.
What does the government do in response to this situation? It introduces a Farm Credit Corporation program which provides such a small amount of money to the agricultural sector that it is spent before the bill has even been passed. In effect, it is technically allocated through Parliament and it is snapped up in a matter of days because of the very small amount involved.
These serious difficulties arise in all probability because of the interest rate and monetary policy which the government will not reconsider in relation to the interest rate policies of the United States. We will see interest rates being paid by the agricultural sector which admittedly are similar to the private sector in the range of 17 per cent to 27 per cent, if the projections for December of 1982 are correct. The reason for this high interest is that there will be a great demand for money.

It is unfortunate that during a debate on an opposition day we are unable to achieve greater response from the government. It is unfortunate that opposition criticisms and some proposed strategies which we believe should be pursued only fall on deaf ears. I suppose the only alternative we can hope for is that Canadians who are concerned about what is happening in Canada and the direction in which it is headed will read our debates and listen to our speeches and apply pressure to the government and all members of the House to find answers to our dilemma.
It is my hope that we can develop a made in Canada interest rate policy. I believe this policy is overdue and that it is time for us to develop our own policies to protect the productive sectors of our economy.

speakeroldname: Mr. Remi Bujold (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today we are faced once again with an opposition motion on the state of the economy in this country. I heard the member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) tell us that the government did not seem to be doing anything, and on another opposition day, he said the government did not seem to want to specify what measures it was taking to improve the economic situation. Mr. Speaker, I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and other ministers, and just now, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), have mentioned a number of government projects and measures aimed at improving the state of the economy. We are being told time and time again that the problem is our high interest rates, and that we should have made-in-Canada interest rates. The Minister of Finance has discussed this matter several times, and has said that our policy in this respect will be aimed at reducing the deficit and slowing down inflation.
We are maintaining these interest rates with a view to turning around the economy, and I am sure all Canadians will realize this, as soon as we manage to get out of the economic recession that is plaguing all countries, not only Canada. As soon as Canadians realize that we are, in fact, getting out of this difficult situation, they will agree that our measures and our policies were the best, in the circumstances. I have a few words to say about the Progressive Conservative motion that says our economic measures and the economic situation are forcing lay-offs and preventing job creation. That is somewhat surprising, because within our own Department of Employment and Immigration, we have implemented a vast number of programs aimed at reducing lay-offs and creating jobs. During 1981-82, through eleven labour market programs including community development projects, local employment assistance programs, summer programs for students and programs for the handicapped, we have created nearly 180,000 jobs. Other programs have been implemented in order to preserve existing employment, such as the work-sharing concept I mentioned
Supply
earlier. We have succeeded in saving nearly 12,000 jobs. There is another extremely interesting program that has been accepted by the Government of Ontario, and we hope other governments will follow suit.
Under the program, under Section 38, we have been able to provide 2,000 workers in Ontario with very interesting work which allows them to keep their jobs, while the community also benefits. I should like to give a few more details on the two programs I have just described. If we look at work sharing, for instance, this has probably been the government's most popular program in the past several years. During the last six months, we were able to sign nearly 500 work-sharing agreements across the country, which means that workers who would otherwise have been unemployed were able to keep their jobs in a number of Canadian businesses. Under the program, employees agree to work from one to three days a week and receive unemployment insurance benefits for the rest of the week.
Similar programs have helped a number of businesses to keep their workers employed and to remain competitive with other companies in the Canadian market. Last week, we had a striking example of this in Ontario, where a company that had agreed to the work-sharing formula was able to get three contracts for manufacturing instruments for other large companies. Mr. Speaker, if the company had been forced to shut down because of an economic slowdown, it would no longer have been able to compete on the Canadian market, and obviously, it would have lost the three contracts it was now able to obtain. That is why formulas like the work-sharing concept are extremely important to all areas in Canada. Ontario and British Columbia have signed the largest number of work-sharing agreements in Canada. Quebec has also had its share, and I hope that in the days and weeks to come, Quebec's industries will be able to benefit from this very popular formula, and thus safeguard the jobs of a great many Quebecers.
The other most important program, Mr. Speaker, is the new labour formula that we are now developing in consultation with the provinces under Section 38 of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Obviously under such a formula, workers who have unfortunately lost their jobs because of the economic situation and are now receiving unemployment insurance can come back onto the labour market and remain active, which means that they will be able to go back to their factories or to their former employers when the situation improves and be as productive as before. Such a program must obviously be developed in co-operation with the provinces, businessmen, industries and unions. The purpose is to create immediate opportunities for these workers who have unfortunately lost their jobs in the short term and wish to reintegrate the labour market. As I said earlier, we want to keep these workers busy so that later on they will be able to go back to their old jobs, and we are trying as much as possible to develop programs in the occupations where these people use to work.

As I said earlier, one province, namely Ontario, has signed an agreement with the Canadian government, thanks to which it has been able to keep or put back 2,000 workers in the labour force. Discussions are now under way with other provinces, including British Columbia, New Brunswick and Quebec. According to our most recent information, the negotiations with Quebec are still going on and we should be able to announce programs for Quebec within a few weeks. Of course, we are all aware of the problems of the forest industry in Quebec and other Canadian provinces. It will certainly be useful to come to an agreement with this government for reforestation and forestry programs which will give positive results in the future and will benefit the Canadian people and especially those who are employed in this industry.
As a matter of fact, as recently as March 25, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) announced subsidies of $220 million for the forestry and fishing industries. These subsidies, of which $170 million will be provided from the unemployment insurance fund, will create nearly
27,000	jobs in Canada. Of course, as far as fishing is concerned, we shall be able and we shall want to develop projects in areas such as the Gaspe Peninsula, the Magdalen Islands and the other eastern provinces. Naturally, when I speak of the Gaspe Peninsula, this also includes the whole North Shore of Quebec. All this shows that the subsidies which the Minister of Employment and Immigration announced last week are extremely important, and this is why we urge the government of Quebec to co-operate with the federal government to complete this process which is extremely important for these two industries, namely forestry and fishing. There is another sector of the economy which is very important and which must also co-operate with both levels of government. I am talking about the labour movement.
It has been suggested that the province of Quebec was somewhat lagging behind the other provinces in respect of the two programs I have just mentioned, because we have problems with labour. Mr. Speaker, some points that have been made are very compelling. In the March 24, 1982 issue of the newspaper Le Soleil, Mr. Fernand Daoust, who, I understand, is vice-president or general secretary of the QFL, is quoted as saying on the matter of work-sharing: "This is not a good direction for the Quebec labour movement." Mr. Speaker, it is my view that in the present economic situation, the responsibilities of governments, businesses, entrepreneurs and labour unions must go beyond individual ideologies or political partisanship. They should strike to create jobs for our workers and to improve economic conditions.
Only this week, the Prime Minister here in Ottawa made a speech on the problem and urged labour unions to cooperate more closely with governments. Mr. Speaker, I feel this is about the only solution for every group across the land, and particularly in the province of Quebec, as I stressed earlier, because our figures show that as far as work-sharing is concerned-and hopefully the same problem does not exist with
agreements made under Section 38-it seems that in the province of Quebec, the reason why we do not have so many work-sharing agreements is because there are problems with labour unions, and according to that press report, it can hardly be denied. Mr. Speaker, that is why I believe that labour unions in the province of Quebec, and in Canada generally, will have to act responsibly in the current economic crisis and ensure that during 1982 and until we can feel and see that recovery, we will have to cooperate with all levels of government, whether federal or provincial, in order that agreements of this kind may be signed.
Other areas necessarily contributed to job creation, namely our community development programs and our Summer Canada programs. I think I can deal at length with our community development programs, because the constituency I have been representing in this house for over two years received its large share of community development programs. In a region such as ours, we succeeded in building infrastructures in some municipalities that allowed them to frequently hire permanent workers, and to make community space available to municipal councils and to every social club or group that applies for it.
With respect to fisheries, we have also repaired, developed and improved fishing ports to enable a great number of fishermen, who would otherwise have to file an employment insurance or social welfare claim to resume or continue their fishing operations. Since 1971, we have invested in the Bona-venture-Iles-de-la-Madeleine riding alone almost $17 million. We have to check the facts and see, how many jobs I admit they are temporary, but I would say in 60 per cent of cases, it makes it possible for some workers to make ends meet, to live decently during a 12-month period and to maintain a decent standard of living so that our area, despite its massive unemployment will still remain an enjoyable place to live.
The other sector, Mr. Speaker, involves of course summer jobs. Over the past few years, I think that our Department has shown that we could take action and implement programs to enable our young people to re-enter the labour market and get summer jobs. We announced at the beginning of January that skills-training program. We hope that the provinces will finally manage to sign agreements for the five next years. With this program we make it possible for young people to complete their training and thus obtain a job which is available but for which they cannot apply because of a very minimal lack of skill. That program is intended precisely for the young, under 25, so that they can at least apply for available jobs.
With regard to summer employment, this year we will be able to provide jobs for approximately 30,000 young people. In December, we announced a budget of $100 million for that program; in March, the minister added another $20 million which will enable us to increase by 10,000 the number of students who can work this summer. Accusing the government
April 2, 1982

of causing lay-offs and failing to create jobs is simply refusing to acknowledge those figures; above all it is to refuse to accept the facts. We have programs for the young, for the unemployed and people in difficulty, which can help them get back to the labour force, and cope despite the current economic depression in Canada and throughout the world. So, in closing,
1 would say that the programs we already have and are implementing are extremely helpful and if governments, unions and employers can work together hand-in-hand toward a common goal, we will be able to overcome the economic crisis.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to say that I am delighted that you are in the chair. 1 am sure you will understand the personal reasons that prompt me to make that statement. It will be a challenge for me to continue when you are not in your normal seat.
In his remarks the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bujold) referred to shared work. In Germany, Mr. Speaker, that is called "short shift". I wonder if the parliamentary secretary has discussed with the Germans the problems it has created. It has been an abomination and has distorted the total unemployment picture. It has exaggerated the amount of money being paid out but it keeps the numbers low. Reference to the more than one million unemployed does not give the true picture which will become further distorted if this program is followed.
I will just pretend that the minister is in the House, Mr. Speaker, although it seems he could not stay long enough to listen to any positive suggestions that might be offered. He sloughed off the entire responsibility for the present situation to members on this side of the House. He said that we are totally responsible for all his problems. He also said we never make any helpful suggestions. We do, Mr. Speaker, but what good are they when he just talks and runs? I think he should stay here to listen or read some of the positive remarks that we have made in this debate.
The minister spoke about spending more money now. The problem with that is that the government has spent all the money over the past 14 years! It took the Keynesian theory and worked it in good times and now, in bad times, of course the Keynesian theory cannot work. The government got itself into this jam and now it is looking to us to get it out. We are supposed to save it from itself, and I think the public is starting to believe that.
The minister spoke about manpower training and the $1 billion that will be spent this year. He spoke of bringing 20,000 or 25,000 skilled workers into the country. But manpower training is a total failure, Mr. Speaker. It takes young people 18, 20 and 22 years old and provides them with an excuse to draw unemployment insurance while they are trying to learn a trade. I spoke to an instructor at Durham College in my riding about this. He wanted to know why the government will not allow them to put young people 15, 16 or 17 years old into a
Supply
proper apprenticeship program; that is the age when they are malleable. Instead, the schoolrooms are filled with people who are not there to learn a trade but only there to collect unemployment insurance. Members on the other side may disagree that this is the case, but it is what I have heard. I think the minister should go out into the community colleges and sit in a classroom for 45 minutes or so. I am sure he would be amazed at what he found out.
The minister spoke of saving jobs but, Mr. Speaker, I have to go home this weekend and meet with 1750 UAW workers who have been let out this week. That is a tragic situation which was brought about by the incompetence of the Liberal government.
Members of the government talk about natural resources, about manufacturing, about industry, but what we are concerned with here is human resources, people who do not have jobs. The government has not taken any action to get them jobs, either.
We must be concerned with the social impact of this situation. It is not new, Mickey Mouse patch up jobs that these people are worried about; it is their mortgage payment, their car payment and the cost of fuel. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) brought in the National Energy Program and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) brought in a budget, but the one thing they forgot was people. They think they can get enough money by raping the oil industry, but there is only one resource that will generate tax dollars and that is people. But that is only if the people have jobs, Mr. Speaker. They are the only permanent tax base we have.
The Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) who is in the House this afternoon, has to admit that she has a problem. In Ontario for many years we have depended on our natural resources such as nickel, gold and copper but at present there is a lack of demand for those products, which is likely to continue. We will not get any revenue from our natural resources but the government still thinks it is going to make millions from oil.
The hon. member for Perth (Mr. Jarvis) reviewed the figures in the National Energy Program. We have all heard them, Mr. Speaker. Each month the situation gets worse. But before I get into that, I want to put on the record a sentence I read in a brochure that was sent to me following the budget. It reads as follows:
Historically, left leaning socialist ideology tends to de-emphasize the profit motive and tax incentives and to promote government intervention.
That is really what we are talking about. Government intervention started with the National Energy Program. That program has done much damage to my constituency of Ontario. I am sick when I have to deal with my constituents who are wondering what they are going to have to do for their next dollar. They feel badly about receiving welfare. They are responsible citizens. They are embarrassed having to go

begging with their hands out. What this government is doing is to the public of this country to go begging.
A good example of that is what has happened to a company called Turbo Resources. Hon. members should take a look to see what that program has done to Turbo Resources.
It has torpedoed Turbo Resources.

That is only an example of what has happened to hundreds of small independent oil companies and related services in Alberta, to the steel industry in Ontario, and to the car manufacturers in Oshawa. It is serious what this government has done. This government has put state intervention ahead of the people. That is what is killing this country.
I am sure that some of the multinationals are laughing because they are being subsidized as a result of this National Energy Program. They are being subsidized with foreign crude. That situation does not help this country. What it is doing is to export money from Canada, subsidize the multinationals on the one hand and take away the ability to develop new oil resources on the other. The only oil resources multinationals can develop are those located in Saudi Arabia, or the Middle Eastern countries, Venezuela and Mexico. What good is that doing for Canada? The National Energy Program is a very negative piece of legislation. It has really hurt the country. The minister has stated recently that he is going to open up the legislation again. He is taking a unilateral stand. He comes out with wonderful words. He is a master of words. I have great admiration for his ability to say so much without any content.
In western Canada we have 400,000 barrels of oil per day being locked in. We import 400,000 barrels of oil per day. We are exporting $16 million in cash a day. If that $16 million a day were to stay in Canada, think of the jobs it would create in the steel industry in Ontario, in the steel fabrication industry in Ontario and in the manufacture of half-ton pickup trucks in Ontario. This policy has hurt Canadians desperately. Interestingly enough, the government is paying out $16 million a day and the taxpayers are being asked to contribute $7 million a day from their pockets to subsidize this totally unsuccessful program. This program is a failure.
What has this program done to Canadian investment? There has been an exodus of 270 rigs from Canada. I understand that no one has been able to get a toehold on the amount of money involved, because it is so many billions of dollars, I certainly cannot keep track of it. I have heard that up to $18 billion is now being invested in the United States, Australia and in other parts of the world. But the real damage being done as a result of this is being felt right here in Ontario. Every day new statistics are announced. We hear about new lay-offs. Then we hear about a pipeline that is not going to be built. Directly affecting the steel industry.
But the seriousness of all this is the toll on human resources. In 1979, we produced in excess of 225,000 homes. This year, calculated on an annualized basis, it will be somewhat fewer than 100,000 homes. We will have a shortage of between
70,000	to 150,000 homes. Think of all the construction workers in Toronto who are unemployed. Think of all the lathe workers, the plasterers, the plumbers, electricians and woodworkers in my riding of Ontario, in Whitby, Pickering and Ajax who are unemployed. Those are the people for whom the government is doing nothing. This government is not dealing with the guts of this country. When I refer to the guts of the country, I am referring to the hard working Canadian citizens who have trades and who are capable of producing a product. Take a look at unemployment, Mr. Speaker.
In 1979, there were 800,000 people unemployed. That represented 7.5 per cent of the population. Today there are 1.1 million people unemployed, but as the hon. member to my left mentioned, the true figure is really 1.8 million. That represents 15 per cent of our work force who are unable to get a job to perform an important function for this country and to be productive.
What has happened to our money? We keep hearing from the government side that our government believed in high interest rates. That is what they told us. When we were in power, our interest rates averaged 11.57 per cent during 1979. Since the Liberals have been back in power, the interest rate for treasury bills peaked in August, 1981, at 20.85 per cent. These figures come from Statistics Canada. They are not dreamed up. They are statistics. What is the treasury bill rate today? The interest rate for treasury bills today is 15.32. The Liberals keep blaming everybody but themselves. We hear them say that it is the United States tight money policy; that it is what is happening in Europe and all over the place, that even the Conservative party is causing high interest rates. That is marvellous, but let us look at what causes high interest rates. Government spending causes high interest rates. The government is so grabby for funds because it wants to spend money.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: What about the United States deficit?

What has happened? Look at what was spent in the year between 1979 and 1980. The amount is $52 billion. Let us look at the current situation. If we look at the current estimates, the figure shown is $76 billion. You and I know, Mr. Speaker, and this whole House knows that spending will not be $76 billion, it will exceed $80 billion by the time the supplementary estimates are brought in. Together with the unemployment insurance problems and all the other problems facing this country, the government will not get away with less than $80 billion. Look at the increase in the figures. There has been an increase of practically $30 billion in two years.
I want to mention a word or two about manufacturing. Ontario was built on a manufacturing base. We have been proud of our manufacturing base. Today that sector is working at less than 50 per cent of its capacity. The Lake Ontario steel mill in Whitby is probably one of the most successful corporations this country has ever had. It expanded into the United States and with help through government loans-I will acknowledge that-it has expanded into England and into Ireland. It has been a very successful venture started by a very clever man who happens to be one of my constituents. They
April 2, 1982

are now in a position where they are not sure if they can hang on. This is a very creditable and highly productive company of which I am very proud. They are now in a loss position. In addition, they have an engineering company which employed worldwide about 40 engineers. They are now contemplating the winding up of that operation and moving to Texas. Isn't that sad? We are bringing in 25,000 skilled people and losing excellent engineers who know the steel industry thoroughly.
I do not know how many jobs we have lost and I am not going to quote statistics, but I do know one thing: There has been a net job loss in excess of 200,000 since 1979. Two hundred thousand proud Canadians standing there with their hands out, and hon. members stand up over there and say that with these band-aid solutions they are going to solve it all. Well, I am sorry, that is not good enough for my constituents.
Look at farm bankruptcies. They are up 93 per cent. Those are the people who founded this country. The farmers created what we have in Canada. I do not know how much longer this government is going to stand still. Almost 25 per cent of our total budget is used to service the debt the Liberal government has built up since 1968. And then they blame us for being too critical.
Shame.

Mr. Speaker, look at what they have done. It is disgusting. The fatal blow finally came on November 12 in what I refer to as a non-budget budget. I do not know what it is and I do not think they do either. They turned the whole thing into state intervention as opposed to tax incentives and removed the encouragement to people to put their necks on the line and start a business. That is a severe tragedy for this country. They removed the incentive to save. The only thing worthwhile is to buy their bonds in the fall at 19 per cent plus. If we cannot get this under control, then next year we will put it up to 20 per cent plus. It is a total government grab which they have worked in here.
How can you expect the private sector and free enterprise to survive with a government like we have on that side? It is destroying us. They say, "Yes, but we go out and buy foreign oil companies". I am sorry, but that has not created one job in my riding. In fact, it cost a number of jobs because one lessee of Petrofina has been ill-treated by that same organization. They talk about mobility of labour, but remove the ability of industry to move people around. That is now a taxable benefit. I have talked many times in this House about what we need, and then they started to turn it around and they-I cannot use the word, but they illegitimized our concept of the Small Business Development Bond.
Let us look at how the United States has done it in the past. They have the small business act which provides that people can start with zero interest while they are building a business,
