speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, once more we have had a fine example of bombastic rhetoric in this House where members of the opposition, as usual, assail the government for every problem imaginable. That is quite something coming from a party which claims to speak in the name of free enterprise. Yet every time a problem occurs they are the first to start yelling and screaming that, aha, it is the fault of the government. As we all know, Mr. Speaker, it is the government's fault that there are some 12,000 General Motors cars sitting on a dock in Halifax today.
It sure is.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: That certainly is the fault of the government. Yes, sir. Well, in a western newspaper, the Vancouver Province of March 30, there is an article, and what does it say? It says, "GM blows it". It does not say, "The government of Canada blew it", it says, "GM blows it".
Read the Oshawa Times this week.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it is not the government which is responsible for all of these matters, but there are many serious ills in the North American automobile industry and in North American industry in general which have to be corrected by long-term policies such as the ones this government has adopted. These problems cannot be corrected overnight.
You have had 14 years.

speechtext: It requires, for example, training policies. However, Mr. Speaker, I go back to my constituency every weekend, as most members do, and meet people in my constituency office, and-
Come back here on Monday with your tail between your legs.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Many of these people, unfortunately, are suffering from what perhaps may be termed structural unemployment. They are people, unfortunately, who have graduated from high school or CEGEP and who do not have the skills to meet today's job market.

April 2, 1982

A few weeks ago, I met a young man who had just been laid off by CPR. He had been working for that company for three or four years, and as he was only 23 or 24 years old, he must have quit High School 5 or 6 years ago, having probably felt that 12 years of formal education were quite sufficient and that the time had come for him to enter the labour market. He had worked, as I indicated, for a number of companies, including, 1 think, a brewery where he worked as a deliveryman, and then as a shipper in a CPR warehouse before being laid off. Well, what did he want to do? He wanted to register for a course in aeronautics at the Edouard Montpetit CEGEP on the south shore opposite Montreal. When he contacted the Canada Manpower Centre, he was told that he had some catching up to do, that he would have to take two courses in mathematics and physics, following which he might be allowed to take a one-year course in aeronautics at the CEGEP of his choice. Which means that within a year and a half, after a year and a half of training and his course in aeronautics, he might get a job in a technical field, whether in aeronautics or some other highly technological trade.
To introduce a new budget at this time would not help this young man, because what he really needs is training and formal schooling to secure a place in an increasingly complex and technical job market. As everybody knows, the government is doing a lot for other young people in similar circumstances. A few weeks ago, the hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) announced an increase of at least $200 million for job training programs. How did hon. members of the opposition respond to that? They said, "That is no good." Their message was: $200 million for job training programs, is not worth a damn. I should like now to repeat in English what I have just said for the benefit of my hon. friends opposite.
As I mentioned, here is a young man who has unfortunately been laid off because of present circumstances. He was working at an unskilled job. In rough times, who are the first to go? Naturally, it is those who are the most unskilled. However, at the age of 24 or 25, what has he decided to do? He has decided to take a course in aeronautics which will last about one year and a half because he will have to take physics and mathematics courses again before becoming eligible for this program. Perhaps a year and a half from now he will be able to find himself a place in this increasingly complex and technical job market that we know today.
When the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) announced an increase of $200 million for job training programs a few weeks ago, what did hon. members of the opposition say? They said, "No, that is no good." Their message was, "It is not worth a damn", and it was sent to Canadians.
Oh, no, we did not say that.

I happen to know, as I have had the experience of meeting individuals every week, that that is probably one of the most pressing problems in Canada today. An effort by business and government is required. As we all know, it is not the Government of Canada which has the primary responsibility for education in this country. When students graduate from high school and do not have skills to become part of the job market, that is when the Government of Canada is expected to find miracle solutions.
We have all discussed the creation of a better climate here. Several weeks ago there was a tremendous debate on parliamentary reform. We all say that we want to improve this institution. However, as I have said on many occasions, the responsibility lies with both sides. The rhetoric that we normally hear from the other side of the House is not really conducive to getting to the bottom of our national problems.
Another example of this rhetoric was evident in the speech given by the hon. member. He made the usual charge that the government's answer to everything is to throw money around. He said that government intervention and government spending was the answer, rather than creating a proper investment climate. I have just indicated that the government has an extremely important role to play in the area of manpower training. 1 would also like to mention to the hon. member opposite that the present high interest rates in this country may just be the result of the fact that the government of the United States has projected a deficit this coming year which will be in the order of $90 billion, $100 billion or $120 billion. No one seems to know for sure. But when our government makes an effort to substantially reduce its deficit-
That is not true.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
-and the financial requirement of the government will be reduced by $3 billion this year, hon. members opposite who talk out of both sides of their mouths are not happy with that either.
I would like to turn to the subject of government intervention and quote an article datelined Tokyo which appeared in the New York Times on January 3 entitled "Japan's Challenge to U.S. is Policies, not Products". It said:
With much of the industrialized world stagnating, foreigners are studying Japan's approach. In France, Prime Minister Pierre Mauroy even tried to win support for Socialist nationalization plans by likening them, however speciously, to Japan's industrial policy. The United States, too, despite longstanding aversion to government economic intervention, seems increasingly interested.
Boy, oh boy! This is heresy! The United States is the bastion of free enterprise and capitalism, yet an article in this great capitalist rag, The New York Times, states:
The United States, too, despite longstanding aversion to government economic intervention, seems increasingly interested.
In reference to the policy of government involvement and assistance in the economy, such as that practised by the government of Japan, Frank A. Weil, deputy secretary of commerce in the Carter administration, was next quoted in the
April 2, 1982

article as saying that he believed that "the absence of such a policy in the United States is a major underlying cause of some of our fundamental economic difficulties".
Another example from the United States is found in a series of articles which appeared last year in Fortune magazine. The first such article appeared last June 15, and the following articles were published in that magazine until roughly the middle of August. An article which appeared one or two weeks before this series started was along similar lines and referred to the new electronic chip industry. This is an article in Fortune, of June 1, 1981. It says: "Japanese Score on a U.S. Fumble." In this article they outline how a little-known Japanese company based in San Diego, California, has grabbed a preponderantly large share of the $250 million a year United States market for a critical component of the microelectronic industry. The component in question is ceramic housings for the finest of those tiny electronic chips. This Japanese company based in San Diego, California, provides no less than 70 per cent of the ceramic packaging for semiconductors made in the United States.
They point out in this article that, first of all, the Japanese parent of this company was started in 1959 with a borrowed $10,000, $30,000 bank loan, and big dreams. I suppose that is the way most companies start off in the private sector, whether in Japan, the United States, Canada, or anywhere else. They set up a sales office in the United States in 1968. In 1971, during the 1971 recession, Fairchild Camera, whose semiconductor operation was financially strapped, asked this company, Inamori, to buy its ceramic packaging plant in San Diego. At that time the company was losing $100,000 to $200,000 a month. That is quite a challenge for a small company based in Japan to take over a company based in the United States and losing $100,000 to $200,000 a month.
While the Japanese investors were putting their faith in the United States and in this particular company, what were other American companies doing? Buffeted by the 1970-71 recession, they were hastily leaving the field to cut their losses. The San Diego plant, they explained, was faced by management, production and quality problems.
The United States managers did not take too well to Inamo-ri's "strive for the good of the group" management style. The plant continued to lose money, so they fired the Americans and installed five young Japanese as managers. These new managers worked as men possessed, the article says, from 6:30 a.m. to midnight, seven days a week, doing two or three jobs at once, even pinch-hitting for absent workers. As the confidence of this company grew, Mr. Speaker, the Japanese began introducing more and more of what they call the Japanese management techniques. What are these techniques? These techniques call for the development of mutual faith and trust among managers and workers. They demand people willing to work two or three times harder than anyone else. They also have quite a technique on quality. Most American industries apparently have a quality control system based upon casual
Supply
inspection or sample inspections, under which they might inspect one item out of every 20 of their product, but this Japanese company inspected every single piece of merchandise that went out of the company. What was the result? Their product became known for being better, for being much more durable, and they garnered, as 1 mentioned, over a period of time, 70 per cent of the market.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, in conclusion, that our economic problems are a lot more complex and need more than just crying out that it is the fault of the government every time there are 12,000 cars on the dock in Halifax, which some country will not accept because they are a shoddy product. I am not saying that that is the fault of workers or of management or the fault of the government. We have all to bear a little bit of responsibility in that. If we could cut down the rhetoric in this House and address ourselves to some of these serious questions, questions of productivity and manpower training, we might get a little bit further on the road to finding a solution to these problems.
Hear, hear!

I could not but wonder, as I sat here this evening listening to several government members, Mr. Speaker, if perhaps 1 was in the House of Representatives in the United States, and listening to the opposition.
They sit there and they talk about the Americans and their problems and you begin to think they are totally ignoring what is happening in this country. Certainly they would have us believe that they are not responsible for any of the problems we have here.
I was interested in the comments the previous speaker just made here, that the deficit in the United States this year will be somewhere around $90 billion. It is intriguing, if you put that on a per capita basis, that our deficit should be somewhere around $9 billion, but in fact we are up to $14 or $15 billion. We will know precisely in another year, after all the final figures come in.
I am pleased to have an opportunity to address this motion today. It deals with the crisis we are facing in Canada, in my riding and I believe the workers are facing the same crisis everywhere. Since the election of February 1980 the government has given us nothing but promises, promises that have proved hollow and often deceitful.
I want to begin by talking about two particular promises. The first promise is one that came out of the budget and was given to us by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). I would just like to quote it. It reads as follows:
The whole purpose of my fiscal strategy is to lay the basis for sustained growth in the future by clearing away the obstacles of high inflation and unprecedented interest rates .. . The policies and programs of the national government are major instruments for managing and exploiting these development opportunities-
The second promise I want to quote is on the National Energy Program. It speaks on the action which must be taken by the federal government. It says this:
16124

It must offer to Canadians, all Canadians, the real opportunity to participate in the energy industry in general and the petroleum industry in particular, and to share in the benefits of industry expansion.
We have been misled by those promises. Those promises have not been delivered. They have not been made good to the Canadian people. The government policies at the moment will bring about those promised results. The interest rates, as they say, should slow down the expansion of credit. They are supposed, then, because of the slowdown in the expansion of credit, to bring down inflation. Obviously, Mr. Speaker, that is not working. The reality of the situation is this, that in February 1982-just a month and a little better away-the loans by the chartered banks to businesses and farmers in Canada increased by 17 per cent. Inflation rose from 9.3 per cent in March, 1980, to 11.4 per cent in February 1982. The government policies are not having their intended effect. They are only hurting the people of Canada, they are hurting the small businesses, they are hurting the farmers, and they are hurting the Canadian workers. High interest rates are probably the biggest evil we are facing. Those high interest rates are great contributors to the farmers' difficulties, which 1 think are best demonstrated in looking at the bankruptcies, because that is probably the most obvious indicator of trouble. The farm bankruptcies have increased dramatically since 1979. In fact, in 1980 farm bankruptcies were up over 78 per cent from 1979. In 1981 they went up a further 18 per cent. What is going to happen in 1982?
As 1 travel through my riding, it does not look as if there will be any improvement. Many of our farmers have been forced to cut back on their production. They have been forced to sell off their assets. They are literally being taken off the jobs they have had on their farms. They are looking for jobs in the marketplace, only to find, as so many Canadians are finding that there are no jobs available.
High interest rates have discouraged our farmers from pursuing their livelihood. They discourage our young farmers from investing in land, farm equipment and buildings on their farm. They discourage even the most established farmers from developing, expanding and opening up new agricultural land which we so desperately need.
Our farmers are not laid off in the usual way, but every day we hear from farmers who are hit in almost every conceivable way with high interest rates, high input costs, high fertilizer costs and high energy costs. All those things are attacking our farmers daily. Our small businesses have also been hard hit by these high interest rates. A survey by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business recently said that one half of all businesses in Canada have cut back on their expansion plans, one third have laid off employees, three quarters have suffered profit reductions, 10 per cent have slipped into the red, in other words, no profit at all, in a loss position, all because of high interest rates.
When we look at the outlook for the future, if these high interest rates continue, we can expect that one third of the small businesses in Canada will end up closing, selling or losing at least part of their business. A large number expect
that they may go into receivership or experience bankruptcy. That becomes particularly significant when you consider the fact that 97 per cent of all the businesses in Canada have annual sales of less than $2 million. In other words, that high percentage of our business is made up of small businesses.
When you see that large proportion of our business sector, with half of them cutting back on expansion, one third laying off employees, three quarters suffering loss in profits, obviously there is not much hope for our future and much opportunity for jobs. What hope do our workers in Canada have?
Small businesses are faced with a double whammy. They cannot withstand a recession very long. They simply do not have the economic base. They do not have the source of funds to draw on. They do not have a foundation to survive a long, difficult period. Already we are seeing evidence of soaring losses in small businesses. In 1981, losses in small businesses were up 46 per cent over 1980 and in January 1982, they were up a whopping 74 per cent over January 1981. We are left with nothing but a picture of tragedy, a future of unemployment and despair.
In my region, one of the industries most hard-hit is probably the trucking industry. Many small trucking companies in my areas have closed their doors. Large trucking companies have cut back to the levels of business in 1977. Some, in fact quite a number, have less than one half the number of employees they had a year ago. The rest of those employees are looking for work in a market where there are no jobs. They have been affected by the high interest rates and the National Energy Program.
Another industry that has been severely taxed in the area of Peace River is the forestry industry. In my riding, there are two major employers in that industry. The first, Canadian Forest Products, has been laying off employees since the last of October. Proctor & Gamble, another company in my riding, has severely cut back production. It has severely reduced the number of private contractors. This year, the first time in a long time, it will not be hiring seasonal temporary labourers. Until now, the main beneficiaries of that temporary labour have been students. Where will they get a job this year? How will they earn an income to complete their education and prepare to enter the job market?
Proctor & Gamble attribute these cutbacks to high interest rates. It is no wonder that high interest rates are hurting these industries when we look at what has happened to our building statistics and housing starts. No one today is building houses or apartments. In my riding, housing starts are the lowest they have been in a decade. That creates two problems. First, no longer are jobs being created in the construction industry. Anyone who knows anything about business knows that construction is often the industry that gets things started and stimulates the economy. Now there are no new jobs being created in that industry.
The second one, and this will become increasingly serious as each day goes on, is that there are no houses being built and no apartments being built. What is going to happen? Where are
April 2, 1982

people going to live? Not only are jobs not being created by the building of houses and apartments, but homes are not being provided for the families who are each day looking for apartments.
I have been told that in the province of Ontario if a landlord was to build a new apartment building and he were to consider his financing costs, in order to break even-not show a profit but break even-he would have to charge rent in the neighbourhood of $800 a month. I suspect that is not only true in Ontario but in other parts of the country.
The question is what worker can possibly afford to spend $800 a month on rent? Obviously the many people on unemployment insurance in this country cannot afford that kind of rent, we can see the trend is well on its way for some very serious problems in this country, problems that are not reaching crisis proportions.
Where has the investor confidence in this country gone? Where has all the available capital gone? An investment in our country would develop our country. It would create jobs, build houses and would restore a sense of pride in our nation. However, that investor confidence which is so important and necessary to our survival and a good healthy economy, has been badly shaken. In fact, it has been shattered. Money that should have been invested in this country is being invested in the United States and Australia.
The National Energy Program, the promise I began with today, said that the oil industry would expand. Anyone who knows anything about that industry knows that has not happened. It is not true. The industry today in Canada is smaller than it was two years ago. While Canada has been discouraging investment, the United States has been encouraging it. What is very serious is that it is not that American investors have returned to the United States or Australian investors have returned to Australia. What has happened is that Canadian investors have gone to the United States and Australia. They have taken money from Canada, money which would have created jobs here, and invested it around the world. Canada is no longer considered a good place to invest, a good place to create jobs or a good place to create hope. That investment image is tarnished and, in fact, destroyed. The result is a smaller and weaker energy sector, which in turn results in fewer and fewer jobs.
Due to the National Energy Program and the uncertainly which it has created, Alsands, Cold Lake and our various Arctic projects are further away from being built today than they were six months ago or even two years ago. The federal government and its policies are moving us backwards.
The investment climate was further shattered by the November, 1981 budget, which was very much like an octopus in its attempts to reach out and grab and look for money and gain control. It was only a swipe at the investment community, our small businessmen and a swipe at entrepreneurial attitudes and approaches which we so desperately need in this country. It was a threat to the capital that we had available.

The budget has been a setback to the development of our resources and the expansion of businesses in Canada. The National Energy Program caused an outflow of cash and an outflow of jobs from the country and caused drilling rigs to be moved south of the border. It is estimated that an extra 10,000 oil and gas wells will be drilled in the United States as a direct consequence of the National Energy Program. The outflow of
10,000	oil wells becomes a significant factor just in terms of employment alone when one recognizes that each rig would employ 30 people directly. All of those jobs could have been and should have been in Canada. The use of those rigs should have been benefiting all Canadians by creating jobs and creating a flow of money throughout our various communities and into the housing, automobile and steel industries. This money would have come out of a constituency such as mine and into the heartlands of Ontario and Quebec. Instead of the economic development which the government has promised us, we are seeing that economic development in the United States.
In our region alone we recently had 60 oil rigs working. Today, we have nine. That is less than one sixth of the rigs which were there a short period of time ago. If that is multiplied by the thirty direct jobs associated with each of those rigs, plus the untold spin-offs to the construction, housing and auto industries, it represents 60 per cent of the manpower that has disappeared. In other words, 60 per cent of the jobs that have been associated with the service of the petroleum industry are gone.
Where are those people? They are lined up at the unemployment insurance offices and they are out pounding the pavement looking for work. But they cannot find that work anywhere. There has not been any further economic growth in my area for over a year. In fact, there has been no economic growth in Canada-our unemployment figures of more than 1.119 million proves that. Fifteen per cent of our young people in Canada, our future and our potential, are unemployed.
If you talk to people in my area about the National Energy Program and ask them about its benefits, they will turn around and ask, "What benefits? Where is the expansion of the industry? Where are the benefits we are to share?" To these people the National Energy Program has been nothing more than a cause of high unemployment in northwestern Alberta. A year ago, unemployment in that area was approximately 4 per cent. Since the introduction of the National Energy Program it has tripled to close to 12 per cent.
Early in 1982 there were 1,500 people looking for jobs in the city of Grande Prairie. There were only 90 jobs to choose from. The job vacancy as shown at our local employment office indicated there were only 90 jobs to choose from. In 1980 job vacancies peaked at 522. In other words, there were 522 jobs which were required to be filled. In 1981, that plummeted to 138 jobs which were required to be filled. As I just mentioned, job availability in 1982 went all the way down to 90, with 1,500 people trying to compete for them.
Unemployment insurance applications in my region have risen by 60 per cent in one year. While this tragedy occurs, the

April 2, 1982

government blames it on the United States and talks about its wonderful programs.
The fact is that people are losing their jobs on a daily basis. What is important about this is that unemployment which is occurring in my region is affecting established residents who have never before being unemployed or laid off. Our construction industry has always had a shortage of manpower. Today, it has too many workers. Skilled people in our region have always been in demand. Today, they cannot find work anywhere.
I have had discussions with our business people. They receive calls every day from people who are looking for jobs. They receive up to ten calls a day and they have to say to those people, "I am sorry, I do not need anyone today because I may have to lay off some of my staff this week."
1 get angry when I talk about this subject because there is massive potential in my area. We have massive proven gas reserves; we have foresty potential; we have agricultural potential; we have silica sand deposits, and I could go down the list.
If someone from anywhere in the world entered this part of the country, they would begin to dream of the opportunities, of jobs, of investment and security. This government has turned those dreams into a nightmare of tragedy and despair. This government has abused its right to govern and has abused the privileges which it was given in the last election.

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Maltais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is the first time I have had an opportunity to speak in the House as parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. I am very pleased to do so, especially after hearing the motion this afternoon, in which once again, the government is being blamed for the serious state of the Canadian economy. Of course, I prefer this kind of approach by the opposition to get its point across, to the steadily ringing division bells which did not really help the debate.
I may say first of all, that the motion is an interesting one if it is taken at face value, and I am thinking of the short-term perspective, but when we look at what is actually happening in this country and we compare Canada's present problems with the problems of other countries, we realize that our situation is quite similar to that of other nations, and that nevertheless, we have made a certain amount of progress. It is very easy, especially for those who are in the opposition, to blame the government for our present economic ills. In fact, the only mandate opposition members seem to have is to deplore the situation. They never feel like suggesting solutions. Since twelve o'clock I have been listening to hon. members, and I realize that one of our specialties is to deplore the situation and find a scapegoat, always the same one, without trying to
distinguish between various levels of responsibility. To give the House an example, I would like to talk about something I am more familiar with, namely, my riding of Manicouagan. I would like to talk about the problems of the designated area of Sept-iles-Port-Cartier, and I am sure the official opposition will have guessed which company I have in mind. Perhaps hon. members can draw their own conclusions. I am referring to Iron Ore Co. of Canada. Everyone knows this company and its president is well known as well.
Is the federal government to blame for the present problems of Iron Ore Co. of Canada? Is the president of the company to blame? Anyone who says it is the president's fault is wrong. I can assure hon. members right now that is not the case. Is the federal government to blame? No, it is not. Is it the international market for steel? This, of course, would explain the problem but does not solve it. Unfortunately, although the federal government, through the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, has designated the area as a special area-there are four others in Canada, namely, Sorel-Tracy, Windsor and Sydney, Nova Scotia-and although we have made substantial amounts available to all kinds of companies and intervenors, it has been very difficult to attract investors. It is very hard to persuade top people in the management and investment world to get involved in new economic recovery programs.
Even the Iron Ore Company, with all its money cannot modernize the pellet plant which had to close down because this plant is already modern. All we could do was to help out the workers directly and provide temporary programs to keep them busy. This should show members opposite that even when you are the government, have money and know the chairman of the board, the problem does not depend on the government or the chairman of the board, but rather on the international economic situation. However, this does not mean that there are no answers. Earlier, I heard the previous speaker say that the future looks dark. It does when you look only at the problems rather than at the potential. The motion introduced today states that the government does not do everything necessary to assist business and promote economic recovery. But what major decision did the Canadian government make a few months ago, not only to help Canadian families, but also to promote a strong self-sufficient Canadian industry? The government decided to amalgamate the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Department of Regional Economic Expansion to bring back under one jurisdiction the responsibility of analysing the economic needs of the country and geographic distribution so that various regions may become more or less competitive with each other. To show that these methods can be extremely useful and to show what has already been done, let us look at the Mitel Company, which, because of a well-structured organization by the Departments of Regional Economic Expansion and Industry, Trade and Commerce, has opened a plant in northern New Brunswick although it would have preferred a major centre such as
April 2, 1982

Montreal or Toronto. Of course, the 11 levels of government in Canada have demonstrated more willingness to fight one another about the abstract concept of Canada than defend Canadian economy. The discussions which have taken place over the last five or six years, and all our actions since the incredible OPEC increase in oil prices are blatant evidence that we have continued to act collectively as though the future held no threat. Only in 1977 or 1978 did we make a direct commitment to an energy policy and begin Canadianize our industry? For too long, our country was happy to export, to import, to have internecine quarrels. It is virtually because of the present major economic problems that everyone is beginning to realize the importance of co-operating and developing original methods for processing our raw materials in Canada, reducing considerably our exports and becoming much more competitive on the market, and in this regard, 1 am thinking about what other countries can show us. We have the example of Japan. Without any natural resources, but with an extremely developed research sector and concentrated technological industry, it has succeeded in acquiring very substantial markets. We have also started to look at the quality of our fish for the domestic market. Everyone knows that, with the three oceans which border Canada and the 200 miles on which we now have absolute sovereignty as Canadians, we have an extremely profitable and substantial market which we should try to make much more competitive.
The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) introduced a most articulated program for fish marketing and quality control. Here is an industry that normally should experience an extremely rapid growth over the next few years. For better than two years already, despite difficult cycles, it has been realized in the area of fisheries and oceans that the fishing industry has progressed tremendously in Canada. As far as pulp and paper activities are concerned, this country of course is covered with forests. And the government has had to impress upon the companies that modernizing their equipment is important. We were becoming obsolete in the face of competition and falling way behind with respect to new markets. Only three years ago the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, in co-operation with the companies, introduced a modernization program. How was it that companies were not the first to assume responsibility for their own modernization? That is a question we should put to them. It is also strange that when the time comes for bringing out a budget, when normal input is requested from those industries, they immediately start complaining, although they are often besieging the government and pressing for grants and still more grants to do their own work.
There are important questions that should be asked at this stage. It is always easy to blame the government. It is the first thing that often comes to mind, and obviously the readiest for marking political points, and showing people that so and so is responsible. But speeches will not give the government and the country a sense of responsibility or a much higher economic
Supply
level. Over the next ten years, the Department of Industry Trade and Commerce and the DREE believe that 5.5 million jobs will have to be created, of which 40 per cent will replace current jobs and 60 per cent will be new jobs. Projections based on responsible analyses dealing with facts, show that within the next five or six years we will probably be short of manpower for those jobs.
Later on, someone will be speaking for the official opposition, and I look forward to hearing his comments. Already, there is a shortage of people in Canada for specialized jobs. We have to import jobs. So there are already two major problems in Canada. There is the need for a much more advanced industrialization in the areas of specialization and with respect to markets and competitiveness. And there is a major short fall in young people. There is no way we can build up the Canadian economy without at the same time obtaining from the provinces a quality of skilled training that would be on a pair with level of economic modernization. One goes with the other.
But already, right in the midst of a recession, the government has to import a certain amount of skilled help, because despite a 9 per cent unemployment rate, we cannot find in our country qualified people to fill these jobs. It is all too easy to say that everything is bleak. The future is much more promising than people will say, to the extent we as a country can take the steps needed to compete efficiently and also to build a strong domestic market. An educational effort is also needed to inform our fellow citizens.
Just now I referred to a designated area in my riding, namely Sept-Iles-Port-Cartier. I have already explained what the problem was in Sept-iles. Port-Cartier has a mill, and offers have been made to several companies to come and set up a business there, but despite very attractive grants, only two companies have shown an interest. Actually, any positive developments will be due to the fact that the government will be a major participant in activities to put the Port-Cartier mill back into production. However, the major forces at work here are neither money nor politics but the need for restructuring our domestic economy and the influence of the international economic situation. The latter, however, would be intolerable if the government did nothing to counter it. I feel that the measures taken by the government which, quite frankly, are often far from perfect, and that is understandable, I feel that these measures are in line with the objectives of the opposition in this respect. I am convinced that the present situation will be temporary, although it may not evolve as fast as we would like. Anyone who is unemployed, even if he is the only one, is in an extremely difficult situation which prevents him from finding his true place in society. However, it is no use making long speeches and telling people that the government, any government, has the answer to their problems. That would be most unrealistic.

If we look at other countries, for instance Great Britain, where Mrs. Thatcher's government has a policy that stresses private enterprise, has done away with social measures and made budget cuts-they now have an unemployment rate of over 13 per cent. After a few months in power, he is also facing major problems, such as higher unemployment and a substantial devaluation of the franc. Scarcely twelve months ago, Mr. Regan in the United States seemed to be the saviour of the North American economy and now he is also anticipating deficits, and it is not because he failed to take strong action. Mention could also be made of Italy and other countries. Obviously, there is no miracle solution.
They want to talk about interest rates. 1 remember that when the Progressive Conservative Party was in power, Mr. Bouey appreared before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, and at the time, that party approved Mr. Bouey's policies and confirmed him in his present duties for seven years. It is easy enough to criticize and speak out when in opposition. But when the time comes to take concrete solutions, they realize it is not so easy.
Another major issue which I would like to raise in connection with this government is the creation of the Ministry of State for Economic and Regional Development called MSERD, which will be responsible for allotting substantial financial projects in Canada and ensuring that every area may enjoy the benefits of the Canadian economy. Often in the past, even if DREE has made every effort during the ten last years to balance the Canadian economy, it became obvious that the economy was concentrated in cities such as Montreal, Toronto, Vancouver, Calgary, that is in large centres. Now, Canada is much more then those large centres, it is perhaps first and foremost the outlying areas. There is much to do as far as regional development is concerned and there is no lack of means available, but the fact is that the various partners must come together. Here is another example with regard to attitude and co-operation.
Let us deal with the energy dispute between Newfoundland and Quebec. 1 am sure the opposition is well aware of the position of Premier Peckford, of Newfoundland, which differs considerably from that of Premier Levesque. If only Quebec and Newfoundland would come to an understanding, the whole territory of Wabush, Labrador City, Fermont and Schefferville in northern Quebec could be developed, for the benefit of Newfoundlanders as well. But while the two provincial governments keep on fighting, their populations are paying the price. But answers to such political problems do exist. If the Quebec-Newfoundland dispute could be settled tomorrow morning, some $20 billion would be earmarked for investment in that area. If this makes some members opposite smile, let them read once again the remarks made by the president of Iron Ore, an excellent source of inspiration for the hon.
member for Manicouagan. They would realize that tremendous possibilities exist. But for some years, the development has been hampered by endless disputes between the provinces themselves and between the provinces and the federal government. If we believe in the same country, if we believe in ourselves, we should be the first to develop our economic potential.
I think that the challenge we have to meet now is to stop crying over our problems and consider our potential. But we seldom do that; we would rather complain about our neighbour and say that we are powerless. On the contrary, we can build something. But we must have the ability to work along with others. Likewise, the hon. member for Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine(Mr. Bujold) mentioned the workers a while ago. We need this social consensus, this type of understanding among governments, investors and the workers, the only possible way to a sound economy. Without such a consensus, we will continue to fight each other and waste our energy. In conclusion, I suggest that the motion moved by the Progressive Conservative Party seems to me to be quite irrelevant at this time and that what we really need is team work.

Thank you Mr. Speaker, for finally calling time. I rise to support this motion which clearly condemns the government for following the policies which are destroying our manufacturing industries which make the things that Canadians need.
The government is knowingly and willingly causing unemployment. At the present time 1.8 million Canadians are jobless and the number is increasing. The government knows that this has come about largely because of its policies, yet it intends to continue with those policies.
What has caused so much unemployment is the government's plan to move Canadian workers away from private industries and public services and to employ Canadian workers to provide the things that Canadians need. The government plans to force these workers to move to new locations at temporary work sites in the Canadian north to dig up the oil, gas and coal and then ship it to other countries. With those products, hundreds of manufacturing jobs that are needed by our people will be lost. No doubt the banks and a very few rich corporations will grow richer, but most Canadians will grow poorer.
This plan was announced by Senator Olson and applied by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and his cabinet colleagues. The movement of workers, forcing them away, is done by the planned destruction of certain markets. This is the plan I wish to examine in the hope that we can Find a way to reverse this evil policy.
During the past few weeks I have been in touch with Canadian workers, trade unionists and manufacturers in the

footwear industries, mainly in Spadina, but also in other parts of Ontario, Quebec and Manitoba. The over-all pattern is the same-lay-offs because of almost uncontrolled imports from low-wage countries.
These past few months have been a nightmare for those engaged in the footwear and tanning industries. Since December 1, the date the government's new policy for footwear began, thousands of workers have been laid off, and the effects of this continued to spread throughout the related industries and service sector. Unionists and manufacturers in my riding see nothing but gloom ahead if the government's policy is not changed. At this stage their frustration is turning to bitter anger as the government refuses to budge. Let me trace for this House the events in their most recent struggle.
The government-commissioned anti-dumping tribunal began its hearings on the Canadian footwear industry in July, 1980, nearly two years ago. Organized labour, as well as manufacturers' associations connected with the industry, were in broad agreement on the type of action required to save their industry. The unionists argued before the tribunal that to maintain the approximately 20,000 jobs of direct workers, tanners and suppliers, effective global import quotas would be essential. The quotas would have to be global in both the geographic and generic sense. There must be no exceptions.
The industry had been engaging in a significant transformation process despite the patchwork approach of government. There was the three year breathing space at one time, an additional year at another, the plugging of import leaks after damage is done and the continual studies to decide what to do next. The industry argued that this atmosphere of uncertainty was in itself hampering the manufacturers' efforts at modernization. A significantly longer period of stable expectations was required for the upgrading of plant and equipment and for long-range planning to assure the survival of a more modern industry which could provide incomes and working conditions on a par with other Canadian manufacturing industries. They admitted that the number of jobs might not increase significantly, but that these jobs would be better jobs in every sense of the word and that they would be secure within the context of a stable competitive industry. They further accepted the fact that imports would always account for about half of our domestic market, even under long-term protection. Together with the manufacturers' associations, they argued that comprehensive and global import quotas should be instituted until the end of 1989 to achieve their stated goals.
In February, 1981, the anti-dumping tribunal published its report. Those engaged in the footwear and tanning industries were cautiously triumphant. The tribunal had supported the position of the industry in almost every aspect of their exhaustive research and especially on two very important points: that the protection required to save the industry must be long-term, and that it must not exclude any type of material.
The tribunal found that our industry had not been able and will not be able in the foreseable future to compete with

Workers in our industry point out that the wage difference between Canada and low-cost countries is partly due to our good legislated working conditions which, unfortunately, are not at present incorporated into the labour laws of many developing countries. The social costs of exploitation are enormous and no one would propose that our labour force should divest itself of the benefits for which it has struggled over the decades. There is just no fair comparison between our wages and those of workers in developing nations. We hope that those countries will improve their labour laws, but at this time their governments are enforcing unfair competition. The following quotation I assure you is not at all out of context:
Imports of leather footwear from (low-wage) countries now compete directly in the middle price points of the Canadian footwear market, where Canadian producers direct about 90 per cent of their product. In the absence of import restraints, the ability of the domestic industry to retain even its present share of the market would be seriously threatened, and the possibility that this situation would be any different in five or ten years time is remote.
That is the opinion of the tribunal appointed by the government. But clearly the government has not followed its recommendations.
Meanwhile, our industry is partially paralyzed awaiting the next moves of exporting nations which will soon flood our markets in response to this opening of the gates, despite the pleadings from manufacturers and unions. That comprehensive protection over a longer period of time would be required to finish modernization and to stabilize the industry. The government has chosen to try yet another angle in its short-term harassing approach.
In the statement of the new policy the minister fairly boasts that Canada will remain one of the world's most open markets for footwear imports; as indeed it does. If the import penetration continues to increase as a result of this leather loophole and a virtually meaningless system of quota protection, we can look forward to losing our whole domestic leather footwear industry, becoming 100 per cent dependent on imports and becoming world leaders in helplessness. This seems to be precisely what the Minister of State for Economic Development, Senator Olson, had in mind when he stated a few weeks ago to the Liberal student club at the university of Victoria:
We're going to stop propping up mature industries that will never be competitive in this generation, like textiles, clothing, footwear, and a number of others.
The new footwear policy, announced on November 24, sent shock waves of alarm throughout the footwear industry, and especially the sector in Quebec where leaders immediately read the message for the footwear industry whose products are close to 90 per cent leather. The Quebec government with unions and employers' associations set up a task force united in their resolve to have this new policy reversed. They appealed to many members of the House. They appealed through the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier), a member of the minister's own party, through my colleague, the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) and also through the Quebec minister of industry, trade and tourism. They got

In January, the task force wrote to the government asking for essential changes in the new policy. These were a limit on the import of leather shoes to 40 million pairs per year and a guarantee for Canadian producers of 50 per cent of the domestic leather footwear market. By this time the terrible results of the new policy were clear. Over 6,000 of 20,000 jobs had been lost in the four months since the minister brought in this ruinous policy. The minister continued to ignore complaints. In March, Jean-Guy Maheu, president of the Shoe Manufacturers' Association of Canada, wrote to the minister. In part his letter reads:
We have not been asking for a favour, Mr. Gray. More than a year ago, the Tribunal found the industry threatened with serious injury from imports of footwear-leather footwear as well as non-leather footwear.
His letter continued:
The only way to prevent the complete demise of our industry is to review the policy immediately in order to include leather footwear in the global quota.
Next week there will be unemployed workers and industrialists here to speak to Members of Parliament about the serious danger of complete destruction of the industry. Although the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) asked for our views, but did not stay to listen, I will nevertheless outline the idea that has been proposed by the leader of my party. Canada needs to establish production agreements in key sectors, Canada needs to establish production agreements in key sectors with multinational manufacturing firms. These agreements will concern the value of production of such manufacturers in Canada. The aim must be to ensure that
production in Canada in key sectors, whether aimed at the domestic market or the export market, will equal sales in this country.
We have a powerful position from which to negotiate such agreements. As the national government of Canada we control imports. We can do as many of our trading partners in GATT are now doing and insist that imports shall not destroy Canadian production.
In leather footwear, the very first step in this direction is to guarantee at least 50 per cent of the Canadian market to Canadian producers. This must be done at once, otherwise Canada will lose its leather footwear industry as we lost our rubber footwear industry through destructive government action.
Canadian workers and employers in the footwear industry are good workers. They work hard and well and they produce good products. They have a right not only to fair pay for their productive work, but also to be able to provide that market for Canadian products which Senator Olson so despises. I call on this government to scrap Senator Olson's philosophy and the ruinous trade policy built on it.
